stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Seedlings of the desert shrub Calvera are rare beneath mature Calvera plants, and ecologists long attributed this pattern to chemistry: the shrubs' roots, they argued, release compounds that keep seeds in the surrounding soil from germinating. In a recent study, however, ecologist Dana Okafor found that Calvera seeds sown in a greenhouse germinated at nearly identical rates in soil collected beneath shrubs and in soil taken from open ground, while seeds she placed beneath living shrubs in the field were mostly carried off by rodents within days. Okafor's results therefore cast doubt on the idea that ______
choices: the shrubs' roots release chemical compounds into the soil that surrounds them.
rodents sheltering beneath the shrubs eat most of the seeds that fall there.
the soil beneath the shrubs contains substances that prevent seeds from germinating.
seedlings of the shrub are uncommon in the ground beneath mature shrubs.
explanation: The old view says something in the soil under the shrubs stops seeds from germinating. Okafor tested that directly: seeds germinated just as well in soil taken from under the shrubs as in open-ground soil. So the part of the old view her greenhouse result attacks is the claim that this soil holds germination-blocking substances. Notice that her study never checked whether the roots release compounds at all. It only checked whether the soil stops germination, so the doubt lands on that claim.

A.why: You saw that the old view is under attack and picked its first half. But Okafor never tested whether the roots release compounds. She tested whether the soil under the shrubs blocks germination. The roots could release plenty of compounds that simply don't affect seeds, so her results say nothing against this claim.

B.why: This sits on the wrong side of the 'however'. Okafor's field observation points toward rodents, so her results support this idea rather than doubt it. It also goes too far: the passage says the seeds were 'carried off', not eaten.

D.why: This is the observation that both explanations are trying to account for. Neither side disputes it, and the passage states it as fact. Okafor questions why seedlings are rare under the shrubs, not whether they are.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Because recordings of the Brenna Valley dialect made in the 1960s capture the dropping of word-final t chiefly in speakers then under thirty, linguists long concluded that the feature was an innovation of that generation. Historian Ioan Maddock, however, has examined some 400 letters written by Brenna Valley farmers born in the 1850s and 1860s, many of whom spelled words such as "night" and "want" without a final t, a spelling absent from surviving letters by their own parents. Maddock's findings thus cast doubt on the idea that ______
choices: Brenna Valley farmers born in the 1850s and 1860s dropped final t in their speech.
the dropping of final t in the dialect began with speakers who were young in the 1960s.
speakers under thirty in the 1960s dropped final t more often than older speakers did.
the spellings found in personal letters can reveal how the letters' writers actually spoke.
explanation: Separate the old conclusion from the evidence it rested on. The evidence was that 1960s recordings show t-dropping mostly in young speakers. The conclusion was that the feature began with that generation. Maddock's letters show the feature about seventy years earlier, among people born in the 1850s and 1860s. That attacks where the feature started, not what the recordings show. So the idea in doubt is that it began with speakers who were young in the 1960s.

A.why: This is what Maddock's letters suggest, so it sits on the wrong side of the 'however'. The blank needs the idea his findings weaken, not the new claim they support.

C.why: This is the trap that remains after you spot the old view. It restates the evidence the old view rested on, not the conclusion drawn from it. Maddock's letters say nothing about how often different age groups dropped t in the 1960s. The recordings still stand. What falls is the conclusion that the feature started with that generation.

D.why: This is an assumption Maddock's own argument depends on. His case only works if spelling reflects speech, so his findings can't cast doubt on it. It is also not the view the passage sets up to be challenged.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Because the surviving autograph scores of the eighteenth-century composer Marianne Holt are crowded with crossed-out passages, musicologists have long concluded that she worked out her pieces on paper rather than in her head. A recent analysis of the ink, however, found that nearly all of the corrections were made in an ink Holt began using only after she had stopped writing new works and had turned to preparing her existing pieces for publication. This finding casts doubt on the idea that ______
choices: Holt composed her works entirely in her head before writing them out.
Holt made substantial revisions while preparing her works for publication.
Holt's crossed-out passages record how she first composed her works.
Holt's copyists introduced errors that she later had to correct by hand.
explanation: The old view rested on one line of reasoning: the crossed-out passages show Holt composing on paper. The ink study dates nearly all of those corrections to a period after she had stopped writing new works, so they cannot show how she first composed. What is doubted is the old reading of the corrections, and that is what you are restating when you choose this answer.

A.why: You saw that the old view was knocked down and picked its opposite. Taking away the evidence that she composed on paper does not show she composed in her head. The study leaves that question open.

B.why: The new evidence supports this, so it is on the wrong side of the 'however'. The blank wants the idea being doubted, not what the study suggests in its place.

D.why: The passage never mentions copyists. You added a story to explain the corrections that the text gives you no basis for.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Engineers have generally attributed the cracking of a ceramic coating used on turbine blades to stress from the metal blade beneath it, which expands more than the ceramic does when heated. In a recent test, however, samples of the coating detached from any metal cracked just as often when heated as attached samples did, but only in humid air. When the heating was done in dry air, neither detached nor attached samples cracked. These results cast doubt on the idea that ______
choices: the mismatch in expansion between blade and coating causes the cracking.
humid air is enough by itself to make the coating crack at any temperature.
the coating cracks more often in humid air than in dry air when heated.
the metal blade expands more than the ceramic coating does when heated.
explanation: Two results go against the old explanation. Coating with no metal attached still cracked, and attached coating, which still had the mismatch, did not crack in dry air. Cracking showed up wherever there was humid air and disappeared without it, whether or not the metal was there. So the claim being doubted is that the expansion mismatch is the cause.

B.why: Every sample was heated, so the test never isolated humidity from heat. 'By itself' and 'at any temperature' claim more than the study tested.

C.why: This is what the new results show, not the old idea they undercut. You picked the right topic but put it on the wrong side of the 'however'.

D.why: This is the premise the old view relied on, but the study never measured how much either material expands. It challenges the causal conclusion, not this background fact, so finishing with the first premise you saw goes beyond the evidence.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Studies have repeatedly found that neighborhoods with many fast-food outlets have higher adult obesity rates than neighborhoods with few, and some public health officials have taken this as evidence that living near such outlets leads people to gain weight. A ten-year study of one city, however, found that residents' average weight did not change after new outlets opened nearby and that new outlets were usually built in neighborhoods whose obesity rates were already high. These findings cast doubt on the idea that ______
choices: eating fast food has no measurable effect on a person's body weight.
fast-food chains decide where to build based on local obesity rates.
neighborhoods with many fast-food outlets tend to have higher obesity.
living near fast-food outlets causes residents to gain weight.
explanation: The officials went from a correlation to a cause: outlets nearby lead to weight gain. The study shows weight did not change when outlets arrived, and that outlets followed high obesity rather than coming before it. That attacks the causal claim, so the causal claim is what's doubted.

A.why: The study measured living near outlets, not what people ate. Saying fast food has no effect is a much stronger claim that the study never tested.

B.why: The outlets were built where obesity was already high, but chains might choose those places for other reasons, such as rent or income levels. Getting to this answer takes an extra assumption the passage doesn't give you.

C.why: This is the correlation the old view started from, and the new study does not dispute it. In fact, outlets opening where obesity is already high fits it. The study doubts how the correlation was explained, not the correlation itself.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Seismologists have often treated a seismic gap, a fault segment that has gone unusually long without a large earthquake, as a sign that the segment is locked and steadily storing strain that a major quake will eventually release. Recent GPS surveys of two such gaps on the same fault, however, found that while one segment shows no movement, the other is sliding a few millimeters each year, releasing strain gradually without earthquakes. These findings cast doubt on the idea that ______
choices: the sliding segment will never produce a major earthquake in the future.
a segment's long quiet period by itself shows that it is storing strain.
the motionless segment is releasing its stored strain gradually.
some fault segments can release strain without producing earthquakes.
explanation: The old view reads quiet as locked and storing strain. Both segments are quiet, but only one is locked. The other is sliding and letting strain go, so a long quiet period alone cannot tell you a segment is storing strain.

A.why: Gradual slip makes a big quake on that segment less certain, but 'never' goes far beyond a few years of GPS readings. That is strength creep.

C.why: The passage says it is the sliding segment that releases strain. The segment showing no movement is the one acting the way the old view predicts.

D.why: The new data supports this. It is what the study found, not the earlier belief it calls into question.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: For decades, inspectors in one region have used rust-colored stains on concrete bridge decks to judge which decks likely have corroded steel reinforcement inside, assuming the stains come from that steel. A recent study that drilled core samples from 60 decks found the assumption sound for decks built before 1990. In decks built later with a local iron-rich gravel, though, stains appeared just as often over intact steel as over corroded steel. The study thus casts doubt on the idea that ______
choices: stains on the region's decks bear no relation to corroded steel inside.
the iron-rich gravel makes the steel in newer decks corrode faster.
stains on newer decks can come from a source other than corroded steel.
stains signal corroded steel reliably in all of the region's decks.
explanation: The finding is split. Stains matched corrosion in older decks but not in newer ones. What the inspectors assumed was that stains work as a signal everywhere, and that is exactly the part the newer decks break. 'All' is correct here because the claim being doubted was that broad.

A.why: You saw that staining failed and took it all the way. For decks built before 1990, the study found staining did track corrosion, so it isn't true that there is no relation.

B.why: The study says nothing about corrosion rates. Blaming the gravel for faster corrosion adds a step the passage never takes.

C.why: Stains over intact steel suggest this, so it is what the new evidence supports, not the old view the blank asks for.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Over the past four decades, a North American warbler species has reached its breeding grounds about nine days earlier each spring. Ornithologists have commonly attributed this shift to warming temperatures, reasoning that the birds now set out from their tropical wintering grounds sooner than they once did. A tracking study comparing tagged birds with records from the 1980s, however, found that departure dates have barely moved; instead, the birds now make fewer and shorter stops along the way. These results cast doubt on the idea that ______
choices: the warblers now begin their spring migration earlier than before.
warming temperatures are responsible for the warblers' earlier arrival.
the warblers now spend less time stopping during their migration.
the warblers reach their breeding grounds earlier than they used to.
explanation: The old explanation had two parts: warming as the cause, and earlier departure as how it works. The tracking data addresses only the second part. Departure dates have barely moved, so leaving earlier is what's doubted.

B.why: This is the trap that's still there after you spot the old view. The study tested when the birds leave, not why they arrive earlier. Warming could still explain the shorter stopovers, so doubting warming claims more than the study tested.

C.why: This is the study's new finding, on the far side of the 'however', not the idea it calls into question.

D.why: The passage states the earlier arrival as fact, and the study accepts it. Only the explanation for it is in question.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Farms along a river in an arid basin now withdraw far more water from it than they did in 1970, and hydrologists have widely blamed those withdrawals for the steady shrinking of the lake the river feeds. Gauges at the river's mouth, however, show that it delivers roughly as much water to the lake each year as it did in 1970, apparently because much irrigation water seeps back into the river downstream of the farms. Meanwhile, evaporation from the lake's surface has risen sharply. These data cast doubt on the idea that ______
choices: the farms withdraw more water from the river than they did in 1970.
rising evaporation is the only reason the lake has been shrinking.
the farms' withdrawals have reduced the water that reaches the lake.
some irrigation water returns to the river before it reaches the lake.
explanation: The blame on the farms depended on their withdrawals cutting the lake's supply. The gauges show the supply roughly unchanged, which removes that link. The doubted idea is that the withdrawals reduced what reaches the lake.

A.why: The passage states the increase in withdrawals as fact, and the gauges don't challenge it. The data undercuts what the withdrawals did, not whether they grew.

B.why: Rising evaporation is reported next to the shrinking, but 'the only reason' is strength creep. Nothing in the passage rules out other causes, and anyway this is a new claim, not the old one being doubted.

D.why: This is the explanation offered for the steady inflow, so it sits on the new-evidence side. It is also hedged with 'apparently', which makes it a poor candidate for the doubted view.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Because elite sprinters leave the blocks within about 0.15 seconds of the starting gun, coaches have often credited them with unusually fast nerve signaling in general. In a laboratory test, however, sprinters and nonathletes pressed a button in response to either a flash of light or a sharp click. The sprinters responded to the click markedly faster than the nonathletes did but responded to the light no faster. These results cast doubt on the idea that ______
choices: sprinters have trained themselves to react quickly to sharp sounds.
sprinters' fast starts come from quicker nerve signaling in general.
sprinters react to sharp sounds faster than nonathletes typically do.
sprinters' nerve signaling is slower overall than that of nonathletes.
explanation: A general speed advantage would show up for any stimulus. The sprinters were faster only for the sound and matched the nonathletes for the light. That attacks 'in general', so the coaches' broad claim is what's doubted.

A.why: The test shows a difference, not where it came from. Training is one explanation, and the passage never rules out others, such as sprinters being selected for this ability. That is an extra step.

C.why: The results support this. It is the finding on the new side of the 'however', not the old claim being questioned.

D.why: You saw the general advantage fail and swung to the opposite. Responding 'no faster' to light is not the same as being slower, and they were faster to sound, so 'slower overall' isn't supported.
